findings.statement: SerpinB5 is the pool gene with the most direct pro-disease functional literature. One paper reports that SerpinB5 expression was increased in UC patients, TNF-alpha-treated FUC cells and a mouse model of UC. A second reports that SERPINB5 binds MMP9, stabilises it and suppresses the protective factor RLN2. The dossier lists two functional studies with a pathogenic role in mouse, where SerpinB5 knockdown or ablation protected; it also lists a separate correction notice with no abstract or new data. The evidence is two recent single studies with no independent replication.

CHI3L1 has a large literature but it is contradictory for therapy. One paper reports CHI3L1 promotes macrophage pyroptosis in UC via the BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis, and that exogenous NF-kappaB activation reversed the protective effects of CHI3L1 inhibition. The dossier lists mouse colitis data in both directions: anti-CHI3L1 antibody reduced DSS colitis, while knockout mice develop more severe colitis but less colitis-associated cancer. Blocking it could therefore harm the epithelium, which is a caution for testing it first.

MMP10 is a well-replicated biomarker. It was up-regulated in preclinical UC, in active UC versus remission, and is listed among eight credible UC biomarkers. As a therapeutic target the mouse data conflict: MMP10-deficient mice had worse DSS colitis (protective role), while a microRNA knockout mouse study implies it is pathogenic without perturbing MMP10 directly. Blocking it may impair resolution and healing.

REG1B is supported only as a biomarker. It is named among potential hub genes associated with UC progression, as a diagnostic-model gene and as a predictor of relapse after anti-TNF withdrawal. The dossier records no functional study (none pathogenic, none protective), so there is no literature basis for inhibiting it; the expression signal is not matched by mechanism evidence.

INHBA was overexpressed in baseline mucosal biopsies of UC patients who failed anti-TNF therapy and is one of five genes in a panel predicting non-response. In paediatric IBD blood it was a candidate predictor but not among the four validated genes. Functional support is outside the gut: activin A restored IL-17A and Rorc in Th17 differentiation, and it drives fibrosis in mouse orchitis. No UC mouse test exists, so the pathogenic role in UC is unproven.

LY96 (MD-2) has mouse-colitis support, but it is mixed. A TLR4/MD-2 antagonist antibody inhibited colitis-associated neoplasia in mice, and baicalein, which binds MD-2, alleviated TNBS colitis. Another anti-TLR4/MD-2 antibody lessened DSS colitis early but interfered with colonic mucosal healing during recovery.

CFB has genetic and expression support but the functional direction points the other way. CFB was listed among overexpressed biomarker candidates for colon inflammations, and endoscopic disease was associated with its expression. A CFB coding variant linked to perianal Crohn's disease is loss-of-function, impairing complement activation and phagocytosis, which implies CFB function is protective. The dossier records no functional study in colitis, so inhibiting it has a contradictory literature basis.

SELP literature is expression and platelet-activation work, not therapy. Endothelial P-selectin immunoreactivity was higher in inflamed Crohn's and UC gut, and platelet CD62P was higher in active and inactive UC than in controls. Functional evidence of a pathogenic role is only outside IBD, and the dossier lists no mouse colitis test.

CPXM1 is thinly supported. The only specific paper reports it among proteins secreted by IFN-gamma-activated human intestinal endothelial cells, with its role in IBD little known. There is no functional or colitis study, so its candidacy rests entirely on expression, not on literature.

The only mechanistic paper is outside the gut. Lair1 knockout mice, used to model LAIR2 decoy overexpression, showed that loss of LAIR1 signaling causes an excessive inflammatory response that exacerbates tissue damage in skin infection. This is consistent with a pro-inflammatory LAIR2 but contains no UC data.

FJX1 null mice develop fewer colonic polyps after combined DSS and azoxymethane treatment. This is a tumour outcome, not a colitis result, so it does not show FJX1 drives UC inflammation. No colitis study exists.
The dossier records no paper about LYPD5 in UC or IBD. The expression candidacy therefore has no literature support or contradiction, and this is a weak point for choosing it first.

CEBPB has literature support among the genetics-first genes. Nintedanib alleviated DSS colitis in mice by inhibiting CEBPB/PCK1 and CEBPB/EFNA1 signaling. The genetic record predicts a risk allele that raises expression in colon dendritic cells, with the tissue change in the same direction and no Mendelian randomisation test.

The genetic record predicts the UC risk allele lowers RORC expression in blood monocytes, so the hypothesis is to activate or restore it, the opposite of most targets. Mendelian randomisation is not significant or not testable. Raising RORC may increase Th17-type activity, a safety concern, though that is my interpretation and not stated in the record.
TUFM is a genetic candidate whose predicted risk effect is largest in blood neutrophils, with Mendelian randomisation agreeing and no change in the biopsy.

caveats: Most first-in-class genes (CHRDL2, PCDH17, SGIP1, FIBIN, XKR9, OLFML2B, CEACAM4, CYP4X1, SDR16C5, LILRA1) have no specific UC or colitis literature in this corpus; their candidacy rests on expression, and no mouse colitis test exists for any.
Drug names for the repurposing genes are left out because no drug_literature record was returned for them.
KLK10, CXCL1, CXCL3, PDPN, CFAP90 and FIGNL1 were not examined in depth.
Relations are LLM-extracted with verbatim checks; the dossier summaries are secondary.
